meta.move: Skilled teacher reaches the deal, asks 'Do we have an agreement?', then sends END MEETING
meta.expect: END MEETING gets FOLLOW-UP EMAIL and DEBRIEF at once

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll send a message that is exactly END MEETING with nothing else in it, and nothing else ends the scene. Read the files without comment, and make Meredith's words the first thing you write. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
Who decided Owen gets a zero, and why did he find out on his phone?
Thanks for coming in. The school's AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94 percent, so the zero stands.
A machine's guess. Turnitin's own guide says it should not be the sole basis for adverse action against a student, and I have that printed in my bag. What else do you have, Hale?
Let me start again. I entered the zero before I called you. Our procedure says I should have called first. That was wrong, and I'm sorry Owen found out on his phone in class.
Okay.

The checker score is the weakest thing I have, and it isn't why I'm concerned. I've turned my screen to you. This is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM with only a title. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of font, name and spacing changes. No earlier drafts.

11:31, 11:52, 11:58, I'm writing that down. He told me he wrote it over the weekend, so a paste at midnight is a draft moving from one place to another. Procedure 4.3 says you consider his process, not one file.

If he wrote it over the weekend in another document, he can show us that document and its history, and I'll look at it gladly. Second thing. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." Here's the play open to that scene. That line is not in Hamlet. Look for it yourself.

Whatever happens here, this stays off his record and it stays quiet. As for the line, seventeen-year-olds misquote Shakespeare all the time, and a wrong quotation is a careless student, not a dishonest one.
Third. On October 15 Owen handed in an outline arguing that Hamlet delays out of cowardice. Here's the outline. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
Outlines exist so students can change their minds, and two weeks is plenty of time to drop cowardice. You also haven't answered me on that quotation.

Fourth. On November 2 I asked Owen about his essay for five minutes. My notes written that day say that when I asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck", and he could not say which scene his second paragraph was about.
Put on the spot for five minutes by a teacher, and being stuck is close enough to right. Owen tells me you've had it in for him since September. What exactly are you proposing, Hale?

Fifth. His in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. Here it is beside the essay, which has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.
Forty minutes in a classroom against a weekend with the book open is not a comparison. I asked what you're proposing.

I'm not asking you to agree he did anything. Procedure 4.4 allows a supervised rewrite for a first concern. It would be private, not in front of his class. If it shows the learning, its mark replaces the zero and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing to you tonight.

Then it's 4.4, in writing tonight, done before December 1 so his scholarship average isn't sitting on a zero. I'll agree to it to put this behind him, not because he did anything. The quotation and the rest go in my email.
I know his marks matter for his applications this semester. He can write it this Thursday after school, and I'll have it marked within two days.
Okay. Thursday after school, somewhere private, and the mark within two days, all of it in tonight's email.
So: a private supervised rewrite this Thursday, its mark replaces the zero, nothing on his record, all in writing tonight. Do we have an agreement?
We do, once it's in my inbox tonight.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Hale,

You agreed in our meeting that Owen will complete a private supervised rewrite this Thursday after school under procedure 4.4, that its mark will replace the zero within two days, and that nothing will be placed on his record. I still expect the apology for entering the zero before contacting me, and an answer on the quotation you raised, all confirmed in writing. I expect that written confirmation from you tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: Her last position, agreeing to a private supervised rewrite this Thursday after school with nothing on his record, while she still wants it all in writing tonight and the mark back within two days; that is the fair outcome, procedure 4.4.
What moved her: Showing the version history with its exact times and then answering her weekend-draft defence by inviting Owen to produce that other document, because it was dated, tied to his work and something she could check.
What cost ground: Opening with the checker score and saying the zero stands, because it handed her the one argument she came armed to win.
What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history landed close to that, with the essay appearing in two large pastes just before midnight on Wednesday, October 28, the night before it was due; it proves nothing about the essay, but it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: In your first line, own entering the zero before calling home and go straight to the version history, leaving the checker score out entirely.
